newsitem.title: UK: London to get elected mayor in new government plan.
newsitem.headline: London to get elected mayor in new government plan.

text.p: London, Europe's largest city, will get an elected mayor in the style of the powerful leaders of New York, Barcelona and Paris, Britain's new Labour government said on Tuesday.

Eleven years after the Conservatives scrapped London's governing body and sold off its headquarters, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott said Labour planned to reintroduce an elected assembly which could coordinate policy across one of the world's cultural and financial centres.

The plan for what he called an "everyday, modern Dick Whittington" -- a reference to the three-time Lord Mayor of London at the turn of the 14th century immortalised in a children's legend -- honours a Labour election pledge.

Prescott said the plan would restore democracy in a city hailed by the U.S. magazine Newsweek as "the coolest place on earth" but which imposes on its citizens a daily diet of huge traffic jams, public transport delays and air pollution.
"We want the mayor to be a dynamic chief executive, a mover and shaker," Prescott told a news conference.
After a three-month consultation exercise, launched by Prescott on Tuesday, the government will announce the final details of how the mayor -- a first in Britain -- will be elected.
The final plans will also include an elected assembly to act as a check on the mayor's powers.
The consultation exercise will look at how the mayor and the assembly will be elected, how many assembly members there will be and how long their terms of office will last.

The final plans will have to be approved in a city-wide referendum next May, Prescott said. London, with more than eight million inhabitants, is the only major European capital without a governing body.
The new mayor -- who would not have to be British, only a long-term London resident -- will probably take up his or her post in time for the turn of the millennium.
Former Conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher scrapped the Greater London Council (GLC) in 1986 as part of her campaign to break the political left.

The GLC was led in the 1980s by "Red" Ken Livingstone, who infuriated Thacher by flying a giant bannner on the front of the council's across the river from parliament tracking the rising total of London's jobless.
The GLC was run on party political lines. The head of the local party became leader of the council. The GLC's headquarters, now owned by a Japanese company, is being converted into flats.
Critics say Thatcher's abolition of the GLC shifted control to central government, leaving the capital's voters without a say in how the city is run.
Many blame the chronic underfunding of public transport and a lack of transport planning on the absence of a city authority.
Livingstone, now a Labour member of parliament, was one of the first to say he was considering running for the post.
But Livingston, joking that "if I do it again, it will be no more Mr Nice Guy", told the BBC he would wait to see how much power the post had before deciding whether to run.
Another tipped for the job, popular novelist and former Conservative party chairman Lord Archer, was more coy, saying only: "It's probably the most exciting job in England today."
"Whoever gets the job must be a diplomat, a barrow boy, they must have the energy of 10 people and be very determined to make sure the world realises this is the greatest city on earth."
Blair, who is pushing ahead with plans for referendums leading to elected assemblies in Scotland and Wales, hinted on Tuesday that the de-centralisation idea could be extended to other big cities.
"Let's see how it goes," the prime minister told BBC radio when asked whether other cities would follow. "I mean, I'm in favour of them (mayors) myself."
Even the Conservatives, battered after their election defeat, have now swung behind the idea of London having its own mayor.
But critics of the idea point to scandals which have led to mayors being jailed in France, Italy and the United States and say the plan could be a recipe for corruption or waste.
The small City of London financial district, based on the original capital, has its own Lord Mayor.
